articles.title: 5 Movie Businesses That Would Be Absolutely Miserable Places to Work
articles.summary: We've all been there. Your boss is a power-hungry mutant tyrant, your coworkers are robots, and you're stuck in a job that makes you reconsider every decision you've ever made in your entire life. Ok, maybe that's a bit exaggerated. But even our jobs aren't so bad that we have to worry about getting eaten […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google We've all been there. Your boss is a power-hungry mutant tyrant, your coworkers are robots, and you're stuck in a job that makes you reconsider every decision you've ever made in your entire life. Ok, maybe that's a bit exaggerated. But even our jobs aren't so bad that we have to worry about getting eaten by dinosaurs, catching a deadly disease, or being blown up by our shady boss. When you think of some of Hollywood's best-known fictional companies and organizations, it's a miracle anyone would ever want to work for them.

Some of these companies might appear mighty impressive on the surface. They've got buckets of cash, tech know-how, slick headquarters, and seemingly unlimited resources. But look beneath the surface, and you'll find some truly terrible places to work. From a possible Fortune 500 company to an military force bent on conquering the galaxy, here are five fictional organizations you would not want to get a job with. And honestly, some of these bosses are worse than your standard nightmare boss.

Serving in the Ministry of Magic is pretty much a dream job if you happen to be a Harry Potter fan. How amazing would it be to work every day among witches and wizards, magical beasties, and spells? You'd be able to use some of the most awesome tech around. Well, it's magic, and we bet you'd see some stuff that would make the average person on the street go weak at the knees. But there's a dark side to this stunning workplace.

First of all, the organization itself has a rather dubious past of corruption, stupidity, and political meddling. As an employee, you'll be faced with mountains of administrative rubbish, unstable leadership, and the sudden threat of having the Ministry taken over by a dark wizard's followers. Just look at what happens when Voldemort's followers seize control of the Ministry: suddenly, it's business as usual for those of us in the civil service, but now we have to work in fear of a regime that goes around hurting innocent people. And Dolores Umbridge as your boss? You might as well just resign. I think I would prefer to work in a Muggle office with a broken coffee machine.

Who wouldn't want to work in Jurassic Park? Just think about it: playing with living dinosaurs all day long. You'd also be studying them and making history. You could have one of the most awesome jobs out there and get to see dinosaurs that had been extinct for millions of years. Yet there's a big catch: the dinosaurs are unpredictable, and some of them would not think twice about having you for a meal.

Jurassic Park makes it very clear that John Hammond's dream isn't exactly the safest place to work. His employees face angry dinosaurs, faulty security systems, and management decisions that seem to go out of their way to ignore clear safety hazards. And after Dennis Nedry sabotages the park's computer systems, its security infrastructure begins to collapse, leaving employees and visitors vulnerable to dinosaurs roaming beyond their enclosures. Personally, I'd never want to be the unfortunate security guard called to the scene of a velociraptor on the loose. And as much as I think dinosaurs are the coolest things ever, I think I'd prefer being a tourist rather than risking my entire dinosaur-loving career on Jurassic Park.

OCP (also known as Omni Consumer Products) is one of those imaginary companies that sounds great until you dig a little deeper. OCP has enormous influence over Detroit in RoboCop and is doing all kinds of work, from the production of consumer goods to funding the police department. The company has huge visions for the city's future, but its business ethics are questionable.

Firstly, I would not want to work for OCP as I believe it employs its workers as disposable commodities, and that the company and its executives are focused far more on money than they are on people's lives. When police officer Alex Murphy is brutally murdered by Clarence Boddicker's gang, OCP doesn't simply let him rest in peace. Instead, executive Bob Morton selects Murphy for the RoboCop project, using his body to create a corporate experiment that turns a murdered police officer into a machine. I would also not work for a company where the boss thinks it is acceptable to use your body as a test subject if it suited the company's interests. Not to mention that Dick Jones has the sort of corporate management style that would make me think long and hard before agreeing to work for OCP.

There are a lot of advantages to being an employee of the Galactic Empire : you're exposed to the cutting-edge technology of the galaxy, have access to large military facilities, and get to work in the service of the most powerful galactic government. However, there are a few downsides, of course. Darth Vader is your boss, and your employer is a tyrannical government. And one mistake could be the end of your career—or your life.

Just try to put yourself in the shoes of an average Imperial officer and see how that day goes. You're probably in one of the most perilous jobs in the galaxy. It's hard not to get the vibe that anyone, even in the Imperial workforce, would be terrified of making the smallest mistake. And you'd be sharing that workplace with stormtroopers, military leaders, and who knows who else. Any of them would probably be pretty upset if they found out Darth Vader had wandered into your department. And then there's the small matter of the Death Star. Twice, the Empire managed to build a gigantic, enormously expensive space station, only to have it destroyed by the Rebel Alliance. Imagine being one of the thousands of Imperial personnel stationed aboard when that happened. That's one redundancy package you definitely wouldn't want! Those uniforms are nice and all, but I don't think free healthcare would be enough to get me to join!

The one I'd least like to work for, and I really can't come up with many other fictional employers that would be more ghastly than the Umbrella Corporation. The public side is a huge multinational pharmaceutical corporation with state-of-the-art research facilities and deep pockets; the private side is all about horrifying experiments, including bioweapons, lethal viruses, and scientific projects that could turn your average day at the office into a complete nightmare.

Imagine arriving at work one morning to discover that a biological experiment has gone horribly wrong and your colleagues are turning into flesh-eating zombies. That's essentially what happens in the Resident Evil universe , where Umbrella's secret research into the T-virus leads to catastrophic outbreaks. And guess what? The company has an even more dubious record of covering up its misdeeds than it does of trying to save the day. One day, you might be in a perfectly normal office, and the next, you're fighting for your life. I'd also wonder whether I'd really want a job where the security staff seems more concerned with guarding company secrets than with saving the lives of employees. The pay would have to be out of this world, right? No, actually, no job is worth being a zombie.

AFFI made its debut in Mumbai in 2011, backed by Hugh […]
articles.content:
The Australian Film Festival of India (AFFI) is back after a COVID-era hiatus, staging screenings across Indian cities through Dec. 22 alongside a new industry strand aimed at pulling Indian producers and investors toward Australia as the India-Australia Audio Visual Co-Production Treaty takes effect.

AFFI made its debut in Mumbai in 2011, backed by Hugh Jackman, and later editions drew support from Baz Luhrmann and Phillip Noyce. Festival director Peter Castaldi now oversees the relaunch. Sitting on its advisory council are producer Lori Fesker, actor-producer Viveck Vaswani, and Vinod Daniel OAM and Sonia Gandhi, both cultural leaders from the Indian Australian community. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories NBCUniversal, Hornbill Capital Back EloElo, Parent of Indian Microdrama Platform Story TV, in $80 Million Funding Round Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade at 100: Massive Minions, K-Pop Stars and ‘Sorcerer’s Apprentice’ Mickey Mouse

The centerpiece of the industry push is the Screen Australia-backed Australian Cinema Bootcamp, which will run full-day sessions in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Trivandrum, with more cities to be added. The sessions are pitched at Indian producers and directors as well as investors, distributors, students and VFX and post houses. Topics include co-producing under the new treaty, putting money into Australian films and India-focused Australian projects, government and state incentives such as the Producer Offset, cross-border distribution, and access to Australian VFX, post-production, locations and specialist crews.

Money is a big part of the pitch. Australia's Producer Offset refunds 40% of qualifying local spend on eligible feature films, and states offer their own grants and attraction funds. Together, the incentives lower how much capital investors put at risk.

"This is an exciting time to strengthen screen industry ties between Australia and India," said Grainne Brunsdon, Screen Australia's chief operating officer. "Having had a delegation of producers at WAVES Film Bazaar , Screen Australia is proud to support this series of Australian Cinema Bootcamp, which provides filmmakers from Australia and India with more opportunities to connect, collaborate and create new pathways for stories that celebrate the richness and diversity of our shared cultural connections." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Disney Studios, Ausfilm, the City of Perth and the University of NSW are among the institutions supporting the festival itself. Ausfilm CEO Kate Marks said the organization welcomed moves to draw the two industries closer and, as Australia's film commission, was on hand to help Indian filmmakers make use of the country's production and post-production capabilities. "Initiatives like Screen Australia's delegation to Goa and the Australian Film Festival of India are a great way to build connections and open the door to more collaboration," she said.

On the screening side, the lineup features "First Light," Australia's official submission for the international feature Oscar; "Brand Bollywood Downunder," from AFFI founding creative director Anupam Sharma, which features well-known names from the Indian film business; and "UnIndian," starring Brett Lee. Indian-origin Australians including producer Chetan Oberoi and Yogi Devgan will also be showcased.

"Indian cinema has conquered the world on its own terms. Australia offers Indian storytellers something rare: a bigger canvas, world-class crews and post-production, government support which reduces financial risks in the film, and a system that delivers on time and on budget," said Sharma. "We want to see Indian money, Indian stories and Australian know-how in the same film, on screens around the world."

Partners in several Indian cities have signed on. The International Film Festival of Kerala will present a handpicked slate of Australian titles and a panel, while Shanmugam and AVM Studios will host the Chennai leg.

"The showcase brings the best of new Australian cinema to Indian audiences," said Castaldi, who added that AFFI is also putting a spotlight on the expanding pool of Australian screen talent with Indian roots.

Lisa Sthalekar , the India-born cricketer who was adopted out of a Pune orphanage and later became one of Australia's leading international players, is the subject of a feature film in development at "Wedding Season" star Pallavi Sharda 's Bodhini Studios.

The company has secured the rights to the life story of Sthalekar, now a cricket commentator, and Sharda describes it as the flagship feature on the studio's slate. Sharda hasn't been officially cast as Sthalekar, though she says the cricketer would like her to play the role. "And the other producers on board, who I can't reveal right now, probably would," she adds.

The film brings together cricket and storytelling, two of the most lasting ties between Australia and India, and centers on a female athlete's story.

Sharda, a Screen Australia board member, is in Goa with the agency's delegation to the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) and the WAVES Film Bazaar . The group hopes to forge alliances through the Australia–India Audiovisual Co-production Agreement, a 2023 pact that lets filmmakers in the two countries work together and draw on qualifying public funding and incentives.

"As a board member of Screen Australia, I have a huge interest in how we tell our stories and how we shape Australian stories for the world," Sharda says. Sharda launched Bodhini in 2024, naming it after the feminine of the Bodhi tree. "The idea is to tell stories consciously and to deep dive into the communities that enabled me to be an artist, which was the Indian community of Australia," she says. The company has already run several writers' rooms.

Also on the slate is the feature documentary "Fear and Loathing in Kathmandu," which Sharda is producing with Emmy-nominated Australian filmmaker Gil Marsden ("The Gymkhana Files," "Revealed – Death Cap Murders"). The film is directed by Sparsh Ahuja, a National Geographic Explorer whose VR docu-drama "Child of Empire" premiered at Sundance in 2022. It charts Nepal's journey from 1960s hippie haven, when cannabis was legal, through a U.S.-backed drug crackdown and decades of upheaval, and links it to today's U.S. cannabis boom. Bodhini is also developing a comedy series about the Australian-Indian diaspora in Melbourne. Its title is under wraps while the project sits with a commissioner.

A Perth native who grew up in Melbourne, Sharda learned Hindi and Bharatanatyam in Australia before relocating to Mumbai, where she became a trailblazing Indian-Australian lead in mainstream Bollywood films. Her credits include "Besharam," opposite Ranbir Kapoor, Hollywood's "Tom & Jerry" and Netflix's "Wedding Season," which she led. She also picked up a Logie nomination for her turn opposite Sam Neill in Australian drama "The Twelve."

Sharda credits "Wedding Season" producer Swati Shetty with backing her as she builds her own slate. "The reason my career has been an oscillation between two nations is because of my belief in representation," Sharda says. "I was just at home in Melbourne and we were celebrating Navratri. And I met a lot of aunties after a long time that were with me. And one aunty in particular started crying. She says, 'You were the first, first of our children to be in the newspapers.'"

Shetty, she says, understands that, having made "Wedding Season" and seen its impact on South Asian storytelling. "Now we need to build on that, basically, as diaspora filmmakers," Sharda says.

In front of the camera, Sharda recently wrapped "Stay," Indian filmmaker Rohena Gera's French-language film, which shot in Pune and around Paris. "As a French-speaking actress, I never thought that I would get the chance to use that skill," Sharda says. "It's a dream for any actor to be able to lead a film where you have to have that one-on-one lock-in time with your director, and it really is the medium of storytelling and filmmaking in its purest form."

On a possible return to mainstream Bollywood, Sharda says: "I have really started to miss it because I'm so Indian. Speaking in Hindi, speaking in kind of the lilts of my Indian self is something I miss."

With a mother from Uttar Pradesh and a father from Punjab, Sharda says the Hindi she speaks is distinctly local, and the inner world that language opens up is something she can only reach in India.

"That part of me is feeling a little bit bereft," she says. "So I would love to."
